[[File:Houston, Texas at Night 2010-02-28.jpg|thumb|[[Astronaut]] photograph of Houston at night.]][[File:Houstonmap.gif|thumb|Map of the Houston city limits]]'''Houston''', the most populous city in the [[Southern United States]], is located along the upper [[Gulf Coast of the United States|Texas Gulf Coast]], approximately {{Convert|50|mi|km}} northwest of the [[Gulf of Mexico]] at [[Galveston, Texas|Galveston]]. The city, which is the [[List of United States cities by area|ninth-largest in the United States by area]], covers {{convert|601.7|sqmi|km2}}, of which {{convert|579.4|sqmi|km2}}, or 96.3%, is land and {{convert|22.3|sqmi|km2}}, or 3.7%, is water.<ref>[http://quickfacts.census.gov/qfd/states/48/4835000.html US Census Bureau facts] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100220105716/http://quickfacts.census.gov/qfd/states/48/4835000.html |date=2010-02-20 }}</ref>

[[Houston]] is located in the [[Gulf Coastal Plain]] [[biome]], and its vegetation is classified as temperate grassland. Much of the city was built on [[marsh]]es, [[forest|forested land]], [[swamp]], or [[prairie]], all of which can still be seen in surrounding areas.

The city's topography is very flat, making [[flooding]] a recurring problem for its residents. The city stands about {{Convert|50|ft|m}} above sea level—the highest area within city limits being {{Convert|90|ft|m}}.<ref>[http://www.uscg.mil/D8/airstahouston/pcs-area.html U.S. Coast Guard Air Station–Houston: PCS Section]. ''United States Coast Guard''</ref> However, [[subsidence]], caused by extensive [[groundwater]] pumping and resource extraction, has caused the elevation to drop {{Convert|10|ft|m}} or more in certain areas. As a result, the city turned to [[surface water]] sources for its municipal supply, creating reservoirs such as [[Lake Houston|Lake&nbsp;Houston]] and [[Lake Conroe]] (of which Houston owns two-thirds interest).

Houston has four major [[bayou]]s passing through the city: [[Buffalo Bayou]], which runs into downtown and the [[Houston Ship Channel]]; and three of its tributaries: [[Brays Bayou]], which runs along the [[Texas Medical Center]]; [[White Oak Bayou]], which runs through the Heights and near the northwest area; and [[Sims Bayou]], which runs through the south of Houston and downtown Houston. The ship channel goes past [[Galveston, Texas|Galveston]] and into the [[Gulf of Mexico]].

Houston is located {{convert|165|mi|km}} east of [[Austin, Texas|Austin]],<ref>Lomax, John Nova. "[http://www.texasmonthly.com/story/texas This Is Texas]." ''[[Texas Monthly]]''. February 2013. Retrieved on April 30, 2013. "No, the rightful standard-bearer of our state—the city with the greatest number of people, of cultural happenings, of medical facilities, of gangbuster enterprises—is located 165 miles to the east of Texas’s pink-granite dome." – The first part is discussing Houston. The "pink granite dome" is the [[Texas State Capitol]] in Austin.</ref> {{convert|112|mi|km}} west of the [[Louisiana]] border, and {{convert|250|mi|km}} south of [[Dallas]].<ref>Martin, Roland. "[http://www.cnn.com/2012/01/06/opinion/opinion-texas-football-roland-martin/index.html?hpt=hp_bn1 Football power in Texas has shifted to Houston]." ''[[CNN]]''. January 6, 2012. Retrieved on January 7, 2012.</ref> [[Houston County, Texas]], located {{Convert|100|mi|km}} north of Houston, is unrelated to Houston.

==Geology==
Houston is largely located within the Northern Humid Gulf Coast Prairies [[List of ecoregions in the United States (EPA)|level IV ecoregion]] (34a), a subset of the [[Western Gulf coastal grasslands]] level III region as defined by the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]. This region is generally underlaid by [[Quaternary]]-aged sand, silts, and clays (clay, [[Loam|clay loam]], or sandy clay loam) and covered by [[grassland]]s with occasional clusters of [[oak]] trees.<ref>{{Cite FTP |url=ftp://newftp.epa.gov/EPADataCommons/ORD/Ecoregions/tx/tx_back.pdf|server=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|url-status=dead|title=Descriptions of the Level IV Ecoregions of Texas}}</ref>

The land surface in and around the city of Houston is composed of alternating layers of red, gray, sandy brown, and black organic [[clay]]; these [[Stratum|strata]] generally dip to the southeast at a slope of 0.06% ({{Convert|3|ft|m}} of vertical change for every {{Convert|1|mi|km}} of distance traveled).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=http://cbth.uh.edu/outreach/fieldtripguides/geologyofhoustontexas.pdf|title=Geology of Houston & Vicinity, Texas|last=Van Siclen|first=DeWitt C.|publisher=Houston Geological Society|year=1961|chapter=Surface Geology In and Near Houston}}</ref> These soils were [[Deposition (geology)|deposited]] by [[Tributary|tributaries]] of local waterways, particularly the [[Brazos River|Brazos]] and [[Trinity River (Texas)|Trinity]] rivers.<ref name=":0" /> There is a considerable contrast in soil composition to the north around [[Cypress Creek (Texas)|Cypress Creek]]; most of the surface there consists of tan-colored sand with small amounts of gray clay.<ref name=":0" /> The north and northwestern regions of Houston and Harris County feature a slightly steeper slope than other parts of the city, with occasional [[escarpment]]s caused by [[Fault (geology)|faulting]] or [[erosion]].<ref name=":0" />

The [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary]] layers underneath Houston ultimately extend down some {{Convert|60000|ft|m}}, with the oldest beds deposited during the [[Cretaceous]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url=http://cbth.uh.edu/outreach/fieldtripguides/geologyofhoustontexas.pdf|title=Geology of Houston & Vicinity, Texas|last=Hardin Jr.|first=George C.|publisher=Houston Geological Society|year=1961|pages=21–26|chapter=Subsurface Geology}}</ref> Between {{Convert|30000|ft|m}} and {{Convert|40000|ft|m}} below the surface is a layer of [[salt]], the primary source of [[salt dome]]s that dot the metropolitan area.<ref name=":1" /> Since salt is more [[Buoyancy|buoyant]] than other sediments, it rises to the surface, creating domes and [[anticline]]s and causing [[subsidence]] due to its removal from its original strata.<ref name=":1" /> These structures manage to capture oil and gas as it percolates through the subsurface; [[Pierce Junction, Houston|Pierce Junction]] is a notable example of a heavily drilled salt dome oil field in Houston.<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://cbth.uh.edu/outreach/fieldtripguides/geologyofhoustontexas.pdf|title=Geology of Houston & Vicinity, Texas|last=Hardin Jr.|first=George C.|publisher=Houston Geological Society|year=1961|pages=27–32|chapter=Economic Geology}}</ref>

=== Seismic activity ===
The Houston region is generally [[earthquake]]-free, despite the presence of 86 mapped and historically active surface [[geologic fault|faults]] with an aggregate length of 149 miles (240&nbsp;km).<ref>[http://www.texasbest.com/houston/geograph.html Houston Geographic Description]. ''Diane Moser Properties''</ref> This includes the [[Long Point–Eureka Heights fault system]] which runs through the center of the city. No significant historically recorded earthquakes have occurred in Houston, but researchers{{Who|date=September 2019}} do not discount the possibility of such quakes having occurred in the deeper past, or occurring in the future. 

[[Subsidence|Land subsidence]] has occurred across Greater Houston, primarily due to the pumping of water from subsurface aquifers (see [[Geography of Houston#Groundwater|Groundwater]] section). This subsidence may also be associated with [[Fault (geology)#Slip, heave, throw|slip]] along the faults; however, the slippage is slow and not considered an earthquake, in which stationary faults must slip suddenly enough to create seismic waves.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070715065340/http://www.ig.utexas.edu/research/projects/eq/faq/tx.htm Texas Earthquakes], ''University of Texas Institute for Geophysics'', July 2001. Retrieved on August 29, 2007.</ref> The clay below the surface precludes the buildup of friction that produces ground shaking in earthquakes. As a result, faults generally move at a smooth rate in what is termed [[Aseismic creep|fault creep]].{{citation needed|date=November 2019}} The recently built Premium Outlet Mall and newly renovated US 290 have experienced the slippage of the Hockley Fault, which was redefined as being farther east than previously mapped.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Saribudak |first1=Mustafa |last2=Ruder |first2=Michal |last3=Van Nieuwenhuise |first3=Bob |title=Hockley Fault revisited: More geophysical data and new evidence on the fault location, Houston, Texas |journal=Geophysics |date=May–June 2018 |volume=83 |issue=3 |page=1-10 |doi=10.1190/geo2017-0519.1 |url=http://www.egatx.com/p/2018_Hockley%20Fault_Publication.pdf |access-date=28 November 2019}}</ref>

== Surface water ==

=== Rivers ===
Houston, often popularly referred to as the ''Bayou City'',<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://urbanland.uli.org/industry-sectors/bayou-city-reclaiming-houstons-signature-waterways/|title=The Bayou City: Reclaiming Houston's Signature Waterways|last=Spivak|first=Jeffrey|date=2015-05-04|work=Urban Land Magazine|access-date=2017-04-07|publisher=[[Urban Land Institute]]|language=en-US}}</ref> is crossed by a number of [[Bayou|slow-moving, swampy rivers]], which are essential to draining the region's broad [[floodplain]]s. The city was founded at the convergence of [[Buffalo Bayou]] and [[White Oak Bayou]], a point today known as [[Allen's Landing]].

Buffalo Bayou is the longest and largest of the bayous which flow through Houston, following a {{Convert|53|mi|km|adj=on}}<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.houstonchronicle.com/life/article/Buffalo-Bayou-Park-gives-Houstonians-a-new-6541659.php|title=Buffalo Bayou Park gives Houstonians a new perspective on the city|last=Glentzer|first=Molly|date=2015-10-01|work=Houston Chronicle|access-date=2017-04-07}}</ref> route from [[Katy, Texas|Katy]] through [[Memorial, Houston|Memorial]], [[Rice Military, Houston|Rice Military]], [[Downtown Houston|Downtown]], the [[East End, Houston|East End]], [[Denver Harbor, Houston|Denver Harbor]], and [[Channelview, Texas|Channelview]] before meeting the [[San Jacinto River (Texas)|San Jacinto River]] at [[Galveston Bay]]. The broad eastern stretch of the river, known as the [[Houston Ship Channel]], plays an essential role in the [[Port of Houston]] and is home to one of the largest [[petrochemical]] refining complexes in the United States.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2014-02-27/houston-ship-channel-congested-by-u-dot-s-dot-oil-and-gas-boom|title=Big Ships Play Texas Chicken in Congested Houston Channel|last1=Arnsdorf|first1=Isaac|date=2014-02-27|work=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]]|access-date=2017-04-07|last2=Murtaugh|first2=Dan}}</ref> Buffalo Bayou's environs are also home to significant amounts of parkland, including [[linear park]]s such as [[Terry Hershey Park]] and Buffalo Bayou Park which serve as corridors for walking and bicycling.

White Oak Bayou, a major [[tributary]] of the Buffalo, has its source in [[Jersey Village, Texas|Jersey Village]] and travels {{Convert|25|mi|km}}<ref name="length">{{Cite web|url=http://floodsafety.com/media/pdfs/texas/hcfcd_pdfs/Flow-WhiteOakBayou11-00b.pdf|title=White Oak Bayou: An Evolving Urban Waterway|date=Fall 2000|website=Harris County Flood Control District|access-date=2017-03-27|archive-date=2012-09-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120904193406/http://floodsafety.com/media/pdfs/texas/hcfcd_pdfs/Flow-WhiteOakBayou11-00b.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> southeast, through [[Inwood Forest, Houston|Inwood Forest]], [[Oak Forest, Houston|Oak Forest]], and [[Houston Heights]]. [[Brays Bayou]], another major tributary to the south, originates near [[Mission Bend, Texas|Mission Bend]] and travels {{Convert|31|mi|km}}<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=https://www.hcfcd.org/media/1285/brays-bayou-watershed110513b.pdf|title=Brays Bayou Watershed|date=November 2013|website=Harris County Flood Control District|access-date=2017-03-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170407145609/https://www.hcfcd.org/media/1285/brays-bayou-watershed110513b.pdf|archive-date=2017-04-07|url-status=dead}}</ref> through [[Alief, Houston|Alief]], [[Sharpstown, Houston|Sharpstown]], [[Meyerland, Houston|Meyerland]], [[Braeswood Place, Houston|Braeswood Place]], the [[Texas Medical Center]], [[Riverside Terrace, Houston|Riverside Terrace]], and the East End before meeting Buffalo Bayou at [[Harrisburg, Houston|Harrisburg]].

Two more significant tributaries of Buffalo Bayou flow through parts of Houston outside the Interstate 610 loop. Greens Bayou, which originates in far northwest Houston near [[Willowbrook, Houston|Willowbrook]], flows for {{Convert|43|mi|km}}<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hcfcd.org/media/1291/greensbayou_factsheetrvsd.pdf|title=Greens Bayou Watershed|date=October 2011|website=Harris County Flood Control District|access-date=2017-04-06}}</ref> through [[Greenspoint, Houston|Greenspoint]] and undeveloped areas of northeastern Harris County. Sims Bayou, which has its source near [[Missouri City, Texas|Missouri City]] southwest of Houston, flows for {{Convert|23|mi|km}}<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vw00AQAAMAAJ&q=sims+bayou+length&pg=SA1-PA63|title=Buffalo Bayou and Tributaries Flood Damage Prevention: Interim Report on Sims Bayou|publisher=[[United States Army Corps of Engineers]]|year=1982|location=[[Galveston, Texas]]|pages=2–1}}</ref> past [[Almeda, Houston|Almeda]], [[Sunnyside, Houston|Sunnyside]], [[South Park, Houston|South Park]], and [[Manchester, Houston|Manchester]].

Houston's topography is further defined by a large number of creeks and [[ditch]]es. Overall, this intricate system of waterways is essential to [[flood control]]; Houston is well known as one of the most flood-prone cities in the United States.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://weather.com/storms/severe/news/houston-flood-history-april2016|title=Is Houston America's Flood Capital?|last=Erdman|first=Jon|date=2016-04-19|work=The Weather Channel|access-date=2017-04-07|language=en-US|archive-date=2017-04-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170419160149/https://weather.com/storms/severe/news/houston-flood-history-april2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> Since the mid-20th century, the [[United States Army Corps of Engineers]], in cooperation with the city and [[Harris County Flood Control District]], has [[River engineering|channelized, paved, widened, and deepened]] extensive sections of all of the five major bayous specified above, with the notable exception of some parts of the Buffalo near Memorial. The Buffalo Bayou watershed also features two [[flood control]] [[reservoir]]s, [[Addicks Reservoir]] and [[Barker Reservoir]], which retain large amounts of water after extreme rainfall events.

[[Cypress Creek (Texas)|Cypress Creek]] drains a significant portion of northern Harris County. The river flows for {{Convert|52|mi|km}}<ref name=":12">{{Cite web|url=https://www.h-gac.com/community/water/publications/watersheds_cypress_creek.pdf|title=Cypress Creek Watershed|date=September 2005|website=[[Houston-Galveston Area Council]]|access-date=2017-04-06}}</ref> through the suburban areas of [[Cypress, Texas|Cypress]] and [[Spring, Texas|Spring]] before joining the San Jacinto River. The creek's watershed, which covers {{Convert|310|mi2|km2}}, is one of the largest in the county.<ref name=":12" />

The [[Brazos River]] straddles some of Houston's extreme western and southwestern suburbs, particularly [[Sugar Land, Texas|Sugar Land]] and [[Rosenberg, Texas|Rosenberg]].

=== Water bodies ===
Houston contains few naturally formed lakes. [[Lake Houston]], an {{Convert|11854|acre|hectare|adj=on}} reservoir located approximately {{Convert|15|mi|km}} northeast of Downtown, was created by damming the San Jacinto River in the 1950s to create a dependable, long-term supply of [[drinking water]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://edocs.publicworks.houstontx.gov/documents/divisions/utilities/history_of_drinking_water_operations.pdf|title=History of the City of Houston's Drinking Water Operations|last=Smyer|first=Susan|date=January 2008|website=City of Houston Department of Public Works|access-date=2017-04-06|archive-date=2017-01-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170124205756/https://edocs.publicworks.houstontx.gov/documents/divisions/utilities/history_of_drinking_water_operations.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> The lake is owned and operated by the City of Houston.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://tshaonline.org/handbook/online/articles/rol42|title=Lake Houston|last=Breeding|first=Seth D.|date=2010-06-15|website=Texas State Historical Association|access-date=2017-04-06}}</ref> Besides supplying water to the city, the lake is also a central feature of the [[Kingwood, Houston|Kingwood]] community and serves as a recreational destination.

[[Galveston Bay]] is a central feature of the [[Greater Houston]] metropolitan area. The bay serves an essential economic role as the home of the Houston Ship Channel and a large fishing industry and is also an important destination for recreation and coastal wildlife. Covering approximately {{Convert|600|mi2|km2}}, the [[estuary]] extends {{Convert|30|mi|km}} inland from the coast and has a maximum width of {{Convert|17|mi|km}}.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2014-10/documents/nccriicomplete.pdf|title=National Coastal Condition Report II|date=2005|publisher=[[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]|access-date=2017-03-28}}</ref> Important regional communities, including [[Galveston, Texas|Galveston]] and [[Texas City, Texas|Texas City]], are located along the bay. While the City of Houston proper does not adjoin the bay, its limits do extend southward to encompass the [[NASA]] [[Johnson Space Center]] and the community of [[Clear Lake City (Greater Houston)|Clear Lake]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mycity.houstontx.gov/home/maps/2015CityLimit-Districts_pj18089.pdf|title=Houston City Limits|date=2015|website=City of Houston|access-date=2014-04-06}}</ref>

[[Clear Lake (Galveston Bay)|Clear Lake]], which gives the aforementioned community its name, is a [[Tide|tidal]] lake<ref name=":02">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tNw0AQAAMAAJ&q=clear+lake+houston|title=Clear Creek and Clear Lake: Environmental Impact Statement|publisher=[[United States Army Corps of Engineers]]|date=1974-11-06|location=[[Galveston, Texas]]|pages=4}}</ref> with [[brackish water]] located on the western side of Galveston Bay. Covering about {{Convert|2000|acre|hectare}}, the lake is fed by [[Clear Creek (Harris County, Texas)|Clear Creek]] and inflow from the bay.<ref name=":02" /> Ultimately, the Clear Creek watershed covers an area of {{Convert|250|mi2|km2}} encompassing seventeen tributaries.<ref name=":02" />

== Groundwater ==
Two [[Fresh water|freshwater]] aquifers, the Chicot and Evangeline, underlie the Greater Houston area. These aquifers are composed mostly of sand and clay. The Chicot is located above the Evangeline, and a [[Aquifer#Confined versus unconfined|confining layer]] separates them from the Jasper aquifer below, which is mostly saltwater.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://pubs.usgs.gov/circ/circ1182/pdf/07Houston.pdf|title=Houston–Galveston, Texas: Managing Coastal Subsidence|last1=Coplin|first1=Laura S.|last2=Galloway|first2=Devin|website=[[United States Geological Survey]]|access-date=2017-04-08}}</ref> A majority of drinking water supply wells in Houston are drilled to depths between {{Convert|1000|ft|m}} and {{Convert|2000|ft|m}}.<ref name=":2" />

Extraction of water, oil, and gas from these aquifers has caused [[Subsidence|land subsidence]] throughout the Greater Houston region since the early 20th century. Before 1942, Houston's municipal water supply was sourced exclusively from groundwater wells.<ref name=":2" /> The inception of the [[petroleum industry]] at the beginning of the century also led to widespread resource extraction around the city.<ref name=":2" /> Surface elevations began to drop with the [[water table]], and by the 1970s, areas around the Houston Ship Channel had subsided up to {{Convert|7|ft|m}} due to rapid industrialization, prompting the creation of the Harris–Galveston Coastal Subsidence District.<ref name=":2" /> By the end of the decade, subsidence had intensified to {{Convert|10|ft|m}} in some parts of east Houston, and {{Convert|3200|mi2|km2}} of the region had experienced at least {{Convert|1|ft|m}} of sinking.<ref name=":2" />

The creation of the district, which enforced a transition from ground to surface water consumption, effectively halted subsidence in the most severe areas near the Ship Channel; aquifer recharge has helped water table elevations return to normal.<ref name=":2" /> However, in the northwestern region of the city, groundwater levels – and, concurrently, land surface elevations – continue to decline.<ref name=":2" />

==Cityscape==
[[Image:Panoramic Houston skyline.jpg|thumb|[[Downtown Houston]]]]
[[File:Panorama of Uptown Houston from Greenway Plaza.jpg|left|thumb|[[Uptown Houston]]]]
[[File:Texas medical center sundown.jpg|left|thumb|[[Texas Medical Center]]]]
[[File:Greenway Plaza from parking garage.jpg|thumb|[[Greenway Plaza]]]]
When Houston was established in 1837, the city's founders—[[John Kirby Allen]] and [[Augustus Chapman Allen]]—divided it into political geographic districts called "[[Ward (politics)|wards]]." The ward designation is the progenitor of the current-day Houston City Council districts—there are nine in all.

Locations in Houston are generally classified as either being inside or outside [[Interstate 610 (Texas)|Interstate 610]], known as the "610 Loop" or simply "The Loop". Inside the loop generally encompasses the central business district, and has come to define an urban [[lifestyle (sociology)|lifestyle]] and state of mind. Elizabeth Long, the author of the 2003 book ''Book Clubs: Women and the Uses of Reading in Everyday Life'', wrote that most of the upper middle classes in the 610 Loop live in the southwestern part of the inner city in the areas near [[Hermann Park]], the [[Houston Museum District]], [[Rice University]], and the [[Texas Medical Center]], while some portions of northern Houston and Eastern Houston have been gentrified and also have upper middle classes.<ref>Long, Elizabeth. ''Book Clubs: Women and the Uses of Reading in Everyday Life''. [[University of Chicago Press]], August 1, 2003. {{ISBN|0226492621}}, 9780226492629. p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=SuMpHvk9G-UC&pg=PA75 75].</ref>

The outlying areas of Houston, the airports, and the city's suburbs and enclaves are outside the Loop. Another ring road, [[State Highway Beltway 8 (Texas)|Beltway 8]] (also known simply as the "Beltway" or as the "Sam Houston Tollway"), encircles the city another 5 miles (8 km) farther out. Parts of Beltway 8 are toll roads, but for most of the route, motorists can drive in the adjacent "feeder" or service roads at no charge.{{citation needed|date=April 2014}} [[Farm to Market Road 1960]] (FM 1960) forms a semicircle in northern Houston and is another dividing line.<ref name=Longp76>Long, Elizabeth. ''Book Clubs: Women and the Uses of Reading in Everyday Life''. [[University of Chicago Press]], August 1, 2003. {{ISBN|0226492621}}, 9780226492629. p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=SuMpHvk9G-UC&pg=PA76 76].</ref> The third ring road, [[State Highway 99 (Texas)|State Highway 99]] (also known as the Grand Parkway), is under construction.{{citation needed|date=April 2014}} Long stated that most of the wealthier Houston suburbs are west and north of the central city, while to the southeast the  [[Clear Lake (Greater Houston)|Clear Lake]]/[[NASA]] "[represents] another burgeoning concentration of largely aerospace-related prosperity".<ref name=Longp76/>

Houston, being the largest city in the United States without zoning laws, has grown in an unusual manner. Rather than a single "[[Downtown Houston|downtown]]" as the center of the city's employment, five additional [[central business district|business district]]s have grown throughout the inner city—they are [[Uptown Houston|Uptown]], [[Texas Medical Center]], [[Greenway Plaza]], [[Westchase, Houston, Texas|Westchase]], and [[Greenspoint, Houston, Texas|Greenspoint]]. If these business districts were combined, they would form the third-largest downtown in the United States. The city also has the third-largest [[skyline]] in the country (after New York City and Chicago), but because it is spread over a few miles, pictures of the city show—for the most part—the main downtown area.{{citation needed|date=April 2014}} The growth of the Greater Houston area has occurred from all directions from the city core.<ref>Long, Elizabeth. ''Book Clubs: Women and the Uses of Reading in Everyday Life''. [[University of Chicago Press]], August 1, 2003. {{ISBN|0226492621}}, 9780226492629. p. [https://books.google.com/books?id=SuMpHvk9G-UC&pg=PA75 75]-[https://books.google.com/books?id=SuMpHvk9G-UC&pg=PA76 76].</ref>
